title: Loss-Draft Clearance Standard for Mortgage Servicers
one_liner: Mortgage servicers and portfolio lenders pay a per-loan fee for verified smoke clearance. That verification gates the final release of insurance loss-draft funds and the end of forbearance on smoke-damaged standing homes. Lenders, not carriers, become the enforcer of a defensible standard.
customer: Loss-draft and disaster-recovery departments at mortgage servicers and subservicers with concentrated Altadena, Pasadena and Palisades books, plus community banks, credit unions and CDFIs around Pasadena and the Westside. Secondary buyers: escrow and title officers on standing-home sales. Homeowners and their PAs are the delivery channel, not the payer.
problem: Servicers hold insurance proceeds on mortgaged, smoke-damaged homes and typically release them in staged draws with a final holdback against completion inspections. For destroyed homes the milestones are objective (foundation, framing). For smoke there is no completion gate: the contractor says 'cleaned', the carrier's vendor says 'clean', and the owner says the house still makes the family sick. EFRU's roughly 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos, so a lender that releases the last draw on an unverified cleaning is funding continued collateral impairment. A servicer that withholds gets complaints and unhappy borrowers paying a mortgage plus rent. I have not verified how servicers handle this today, so this is the riskiest assumption to test first.
solution: A one-page, servicer-adoptable 'Smoke Clearance Acceptance Standard' covering sampling grid, threshold basis, chain of custody and lab accreditation, tied to AB 1795, AIHA and IICRC/RIA/CIRI references and versioned for DTSC's 2028-29 standards. Alongside it, a portal where the borrower's hygienist or remediator uploads results. We verify them (automated checks plus partner CIH-of-record review) and issue a machine-readable Clearance Verification (pass, fail, or specific deficiency list) that the servicer's loss-draft workflow accepts to release the final draw or convert a forbearance. A book-level ledger shows every loan in the burn perimeter, joined to parcels, with status: not tested, tested, remediating, cleared. Testing stays paid by the insurer under AB 1795 or by the borrower from claim proceeds. The servicer pays only for verification and monitoring.
why_now: AB 1795 (effective 1/1/2027) forces insurers to pay for testing and bars ALE termination before clearance, so a verified clearance event now exists in statute and can be a lender milestone. 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage in the LA fires, many mortgaged, are hitting the remediation and final-draw stage through 2027. Meanwhile the state standard will not exist until 2028-29, and servicers adopt vendor standards faster than agencies write them.
revenue_model: Servicers pay $250-$450 per loan verified, usually recoverable as an inspection or protective-advance line they already charge, plus $2-$5 per loan per month for ledger monitoring on flagged loans. Community banks and credit unions pay a flat $15k pilot. Hygienists and remediators can pay $50 to have their evidence pack pre-checked against the standard, since a fail costs them time. Honest sizing: LA alone is roughly 13,000 homes x about 55% mortgaged x $350 x 1.5 verifications, or about $3.7M. The business is the repeatable template for post-disaster loss-draft verification (hurricane mold, flood, wildfire) across the US, not California smoke alone.
non_obvious_insight: The party with real power over whether a smoke repair is 'done' is not the carrier or the state. It is whoever holds the last check. Servicers already control disbursement, already buy standardized inspection work in bulk, and do not need to win the sampling-design argument. They need a pass/fail they can rely on. Lender incentives also align with policyholders (impaired collateral) and with carriers (fewer reopened claims and bad-faith suits), which neutralizes the parent's buyer conflict. If five servicers and credit unions accept the same evidence package, contractors and hygienists will produce to it, so the de facto standard is set by lenders.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ask 5 public adjusters which servicers are sitting on their clients' checks, then hold 25 calls with loss-draft and disaster managers at about 10 servicers and 10 Pasadena-area banks and credit unions. The one question is what evidence would let you release the final draw on a smoke claim. Days 10-20: draft the one-page acceptance standard and get two CIHs and one toxicologist to endorse it publicly. Days 20-30: agree a paid pilot of 15-30 loans at about $300 with one credit union or servicer, and pre-check evidence packs for 10 borrowers referred by PAs. If no servicer says smoke draws are actually stuck, kill or pivot to escrow and title on resale.
lineage: mutation of I0715 ('Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms sell assessments to insurers and homeowners and none sells into loan servicing. They become the channel: the ones that produce evidence to our standard win a document lenders accept. Sedgwick and other carrier TPAs are structurally carrier-side, and a lender will not accept a carrier-side attestation as proof of collateral condition. The IICRC and AIHA guides and the Purdue and EFRU resources are cited inside the acceptance criteria, so they are inputs, not rivals. The state's 2028-29 standards make our criteria more specific, not obsolete, because servicers still need a verification workflow. The adjacent risk is property-preservation and loss-draft inspection vendors, who lack IH capability. We would license the standard to them white-label rather than compete.

title: Remote Load Calcs That Avoid Panel Upgrades
one_liner: A photo-and-utility-bill service that proves an existing electrical panel can take a heat pump or EV charger, with load-management devices when it cannot.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger installers and solar-plus-storage installers without in-house electricians. Later: state and utility electrification programs.
problem: Data centers are absorbing electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months). Residential electrician time becomes the scarcest input, so panel upgrades stall every electrification job. HVAC contractors selling heat pumps are blocked by work they do not do and cannot schedule. The HVAC rebound expected in 2027 will make it worse.
solution: Installer uploads a photo of the panel label plus 12 months of utility data. The service returns a permit-ready load calculation under the existing-load method, stamped by a remote licensed engineer or electrician. It recommends the cheapest path: no upgrade, a load-management or circuit-pausing device allowed by recent NEC editions, or a smart panel, with the material list for the installer's quote.
why_now: Electrician scarcity from data-center overtime ($130-170K, vendor stat), 2027 HVAC rebound with A2L certification adding friction, and a 110K technician shortage. Load-management devices and energy-management provisions are now commercially available and code-recognized in many places.
revenue_model: $79-149 per calculation billed to installers. Annual contracts with programs. Referral margin from load-management device makers.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for electrification is neither the heat pump nor the HVAC tech, it is the panel and the electrician-days it consumes. Avoiding electrician hours is worth more than adding them, and the existing truck-roll panel check can be done as a $99 desk job by one remote engineer serving many installers.
first_30_days: Sign 20 HVAC contractors in one state. Contract a licensed PE or master electrician for templates and stamps. Deliver 50 calculations by hand. Measure the percentage that avoided an upgrade.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TrueLoad (eTherm Solutions LLC), TradesQuote (rajesh99/tradesquote-website), PanelWright (open source), SPAN (PowerUp / smart panel). White space: The market is not empty: TrueLoad already sells software-only NEC 220.87 reports from utility interval data to heat pump and EV installers at $30/project, and the underlying calc is even open-source. The white space is what TrueLoad says it does not do, plus the liability-bearing layer nobody has bundled. (1) A stamped, licensed-professional deliverable. Small HVAC and EV contractors without in-house electricians must take on risk when they self-certify a software report, and WattMonk shows they pay for stamped desk work in solar. (2) Photo-of-panel intake, so installers do not hand-key service details. (3) A cheapest-path recommendation with a compliant load-management spec and bill of materials (NEC 625.42 EVEMS, 750 energy management, 705.13 power control systems), which TrueLoad explicitly lacks and hardware vendors only offer for their own products. (4) Doing the utility interval-data retrieval for the contractor, which is the real friction, since TrueLoad's own guides tell users to request it themselves. (5) HVAC and heat-pump contractors as the buyer, with a pre-check integrated into state or utility programs. Weak points: a $79-149 price against a $30 software anchor needs the stamp and outcome to justify a 3-5x premium; solar desks like WattMonk or Aurora can add this as a SKU; and I could not verify Qmerit or unknown small engineering shops.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
customer: Florida condo associations and the licensed engineers and property managers who run their milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies; secondary buyers are master-policy underwriters, lenders and buyers' agents doing condo diligence.
problem: Carriers want structural documents before they bind a master policy, SIRS and milestone inspections are mandatory for 3+ story buildings, and special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit. Boards cannot tell whether their building is stable or sinking until an engineer bills for scoping. A 2024 University of Miami InSAR study found 35 Miami Beach to Sunny Isles buildings subsiding 2-8 cm over 2016-2023, and no commercial product packages this for boards.
solution: Process free Sentinel-1 radar (2015 onward), ESA archive radar for the 1990s-2010s, and newly public NISAR L-band data into a per-building vertical-motion trend. Add differential tilt across the footprint and a comparison against neighbours built on similar fill. Deliver a 3-page Settlement Passport plus a monitoring feed, positioned as a screening indicator that sharpens inspection scope, with an engineer partner signing off. It is not a substitute for the inspection.
why_now: Florida's post-Surfside SB 4-D inspection and reserve-study mandates are now enforced and carriers demand documents. NISAR L-band data has been free through ASF since the July 20, 2026 public release, adding to the Sentinel-1 record. Peer-reviewed proof that InSAR resolves individual Miami towers exists but has not been productized. Reinsurance is softening while condo retail insurance is still squeezed.
revenue_model: $900-$2,500 per building for the initial passport and $300/yr for monitoring. Wholesale price of about $400 to engineering firms who bundle it into SIRS work. $100/building/yr portfolio contracts for management companies.
non_obvious_insight: InSAR is treated as an academic or pipeline-monitoring tool, but the buyer with a legal deadline and a real budget is a condo board that must assemble a structural file. Persistent-scatterer InSAR works best on concrete high-rises, the exact asset at issue. The 10-30 year archive can also show a building has been stable for decades, which makes it a positive underwriting asset for the many buildings that are fine, not just a warning label.
first_30_days: Run the free Sentinel-1 stack for about 400 buildings on the Miami-Dade and Broward barrier islands. Offer one free passport to each of 15 engineering firms and 5 management companies, and sign 2 engineers as resellers. Then charge the first 10 boards facing reserve-study or insurance-renewal deadlines.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Estructura (division of Dorado Services) - TerraIntel InSAR + GeoSIG sensors + GeoSMART, TRE ALTAMIRA (CLS Group; TRE Altamira Inc.), Sixense Satellite / Atlas InSAR (Vinci group), Fugro (InSAR high-rise settlement evaluation and prediction). White space: No one found sells a productized, fixed-price, board-readable per-building InSAR settlement history for Florida condo towers, wholesaled to the engineers who already write milestone and SIRS reports. The InSAR firms (TRE Altamira, Sixense, Fugro, SkyGeo, Detektia) sell quote-based enterprise projects. SatSense does per-property InSAR but for the UK. Estructura (June 2026) pitches InSAR to condos but only as one part of a sensor bundle, with no disclosed price and no report artifact. The Florida condo-data players (Domexa, CondoScan, CleanCondo, PropFusion) have no physical-movement data. Specifically unserved: (1) a $400-$2,500 report an engineer can attach to a Phase 1 milestone inspection or SIRS; (2) a 10-30 year ERS/Envisat/Sentinel-1 history that shows a building is stable, for lenders and underwriters; (3) a pre-construction baseline for a neighbouring tower's pile driving; (4) a roll-up for management companies with many buildings. A strong caveat is that this is not a technology moat. TRE Altamira already processed this exact coastline, ISCE, MintPy and StaMPS are open source, and OPERA gives a free coarse baseline. Any incumbent or Estructura could productize this quickly, so the wedge is distribution through engineers, engineer sign-off, and price.

title: Courtroom ETA: Call-Time Network for Family Court
one_liner: A 'FlightAware for family court calendars' that texts litigants, lawyers and freelance reporters and interpreters their predicted call time, giving the queue away and selling the same feed to the professionals who lose half-day minimums waiting.
customer: Start: DV survivors and family litigants (free, via legal-aid and DV org sponsors) and solo family-law attorneys ($29/month). Paying side by month 6: freelance court reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys who buy call-time alerts to hop between hearings. Later: courts, which pay for staggered 'time-certain' calendars.
problem: Family calendars run on the 8:30 cattle call: 30-40 matters set at one time and called in an order nobody can see. Parties, including survivors who may wait near their abuser, sit in a hallway for hours. Attorneys burn billable time (a solo lawyer's 2-hour wait costs $400-600, an assumption to verify). Reporters, interpreters and appearance counsel price by the half day because no one can predict a 15-minute call time. The parent's dispatch model needed that prediction but assumed it was a feature, when it is the missing infrastructure for every short-hearing service.
solution: Inverted product: prediction first, services second. Month 1-6 product: an SMS bot for two departments in one courthouse. A litigant or attorney texts a case number and gets 'about 45 minutes; you are 9th of 34'. Data comes from the public daily calendar, historical durations by hearing type and judge, and check-ins: people text 'called' or 'out' from the hallway (not from inside the courtroom, where phones may be restricted), plus paid spotters logging call order at $18/hour for the first 20 court days. Publish a per-department 'wait report card' as press and leverage. The same feed then powers a services layer, with reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys buying alerts and booking one hearing at a time, which turns the parent's marketplace into the second product. Endgame: the call-time index becomes the standard that courts license to stagger calendars.
why_now: After the FVAP decision the gap in recorded hearings is public news. Courts, legal aid and press now treat family-court process failures as a story. Cheap SMS, LLM-based calendar parsing and speech-to-text make the data layer nearly free, while calendar data has been public but unused for years. The reporter shortage forces reporters to hop to survive, and the shortage gives them an incentive to pay for the ETA.
revenue_model: Free for litigants (sponsored by DV legal aid, foundation and IOLTA-type grants). $29/month for attorneys. $99-299/month per reporter, interpreter or appearance attorney for alerts and hop scheduling, plus a booking fee (10-15%) once the per-hearing marketplace exists. Courts pay for calendar analytics and a staggering tool ($20-60K per court per year, an assumption) after the wait report cards create pressure. Bottom-up illustration to test: 40 family departments x 30 matters x 2 parties is about 2,400 party-attendances/day in one large county.
non_obvious_insight: The reporting shortage is a symptom of an information problem: half-day minimums exist because the call time is unknowable. Give the information away to the crowd and charge the people who can turn it into utilization. Each check-in improves the ETA for everyone else in the department (network effect), so density in a courthouse is the moat, and the data is a cornered resource no reporter agency can copy without the crowd. It also fixes the parent's legal flaw: it needs no remote reporting, only public calendars and voluntary check-ins.
first_30_days: Week 1: choose the two busiest family departments in one large county, hire two spotters (retired court watchers or paralegal students) and log call order and durations for 20 court days. Week 2: build a Twilio SMS bot with a manual ETA rule (calendar position x median duration by hearing type). Week 3: recruit 10 solo attorneys and 2 DV legal-aid groups as first users, and 3 freelance interpreters or reporters as paying alerts customers. Week 4: publish the first department wait report card and test whether hallway wait shrinks and whether any reporter will pay $99/month. Day 180 target: 300 active attorneys and litigants in one courthouse, 20 paying professionals, and a second courthouse.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors predicts call time. Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout are booking marketplaces for depositions and would be buyers of the feed, not rivals. Incumbent agencies sell half-day pro tem, which is what the ETA erodes. eScribers and Verbit handle records after the fact, and the AB 3013 pilot is court-employed reporting. The one adjacent category I could not check (search budget exhausted) is court-date reminder apps, which remind people of the date but, as far as I know, do not rank queue position within a calendar. Verify that before building. Main risks: courts restricting phone use or check-ins, and calendar data quality, so the first release relies on spotters and public calendars.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arcadia (utility data platform), UtilityAPI, Wint Water Intelligence, SmartRent. White space: I found no product that does what this idea proposes: rules on owner-authorized utility interval data to detect squatters, unauthorized occupancy, leaks and HVAC problems in vacant units, then produce a carrier-formatted vacancy-inspection log with no installed hardware. The alternatives are hardware (Wint, SmartRent, Minut, Flume), utility data plumbing (Arcadia, UtilityAPI), or bill-management tools (Conservice, EnergyCAP). None of their pages pitch vacant-unit security or insurance vacancy compliance. Three things are genuinely unserved: (1) electric-baseline occupancy detection in a vacant unit, which the water-focused players cannot do; (2) an inspection log formatted for carrier vacancy-permit conditions; (3) small portfolios of 100 to 2,000 doors, which Wint and SmartRent do not serve well. I could not find how commonly PMs use utility-supplied continuous-flow leak alerts (water utilities with AMI portals, my background knowledge, unverified). Research limits: the WebSearch budget was used up, so no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches were possible. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and background knowledge, and the absence of a direct competitor is not proven. Main risks: (a) UtilityAPI lists $2.40 to $30 per meter per month for scheduled monitoring, so on a $1 to $2 per door or $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month price, data cost could exceed revenue unless you use free Green Button Connect direct integrations or price higher; (b) interval water data through third-party APIs is thin, because most water utilities have no Green Button Connect, and leaks are the biggest loss, so the water rule may only work in a few metros; (c) each owner must authorize each utility account, a real onboarding cost at 100 to 2,000 doors; (d) I found nothing showing carriers accept a monitoring log in place of a vacancy permit or endorsement, so the 'log preserves coverage' claim is unproven; (e) the '48-hour trespass window' insight is unverified. The Florida HB 621 page I fetched confirms sheriff removal and a July 1, 2024 effective date but gives no time threshold, and Wikipedia confirms Alabama's 2024 24-hour removal law, so statute-specific timing needs a lawyer.

title: Carve-Out Audit Kit for Challenger ASC Billers
one_liner: A white-label implant carve-out engine for independent ASC billing companies, who use a free lookback on a prospect or new client as their sales weapon and split the recovered dollars with us.
customer: Independent ASC billing and RCM companies with roughly 8-60 ASC clients. These are the long tail behind SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble. The buyer is the owner or head of sales. The ASC still pays the fee, but through its biller.
problem: Billers win ASC clients on percentage fee and references, and the new-ASC wave makes that fight harder. They can't afford implant analysts or invoice-parsing tooling for 30 clients. A startup selling direct to ASCs hits a trust wall, because owners won't hand 835s and contracts to an unknown vendor. Billers already hold the BAAs, the ERA feeds and the contract PDFs. Billers also don't buy 'recovery', because it admits past misses. They buy client acquisition and retention.
solution: White-label 'Carve-Out Desk' with three parts. (1) Lookback as an RFP weapon. For a prospect, or a new client in its first 30 days, ingest 12-24 months of 835s, implant log and AP invoices and return a co-branded Carve-Out Leak Report showing dollars by payer and CPT. The new biller can recover the prior biller's misses with no political cost. (2) Recovery ops. We prepare attachment packets and corrected claims and appeals, and the biller submits, or we do so under the biller's credentials. (3) A prospective pre-bill gate, delivered as upload plus a review queue that works with whichever PM system the biller's clients use, checking invoice attached and L8699/027x coded to trigger the carve-out. Each partner audit adds payer-clause entries to a shared clause library.
why_now: New and converting spine and ortho ASCs are choosing billers now, as CMS's CY2026 ASC rule (CMS-1834-FC) reportedly expands the ASC list; verify the exact list. Payer AI payment integrity makes attachment mistakes costly. Invoice parsing now costs cents, so the audit can be run for a prospect who has not yet signed. Becker's coverage in 2026 shows implant cost is the hot ASC topic, so billers have a live sales angle.
revenue_model: Money flow: the payer pays the ASC as usual. The ASC pays the biller 25-30% of recovered carve-out dollars under a 'Carve-Out Assurance' schedule the biller adds to its contract. The biller remits about 50-60% of that to us, so we take roughly 15% of recovered dollars and the biller keeps roughly 10-12% for near-zero labor. On top, $300-600 per facility per month for the pre-bill gate and a $2-4k flat fee per prospect lookback, credited against the rev-share. Illustrative unit economics, to be verified in pilots: a facility recovering $240k in year one yields about $36k to us plus about $6k of platform fees. Twenty partners with an average of 20 implant-heavy clients each is 400 facilities, which supports a $5-10M ARR outcome.
non_obvious_insight: The biller's incentives are the opposite of the ASC's. Incumbents will not audit themselves, but their challengers desperately want a proof-of-value opener. title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion

Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful. title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.
customer: State SNAP and Medicaid policy directors and eligibility-system program managers (the people running user-acceptance testing), then the system integrators that build the systems and the AI-tool vendors selling into agencies. First buyers: 2-3 states whose H.R.1 system releases are due between Oct 2026 and Jan 2027 and that already have a UAT process.
problem: The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times, which no worker training can fix. NC's eligibility system stacked shelter deductions when caseworkers updated rent, and a one-click prompt fixed it and has since been used more than 20,000 times. H.R.1 forces reprogramming everywhere at once (SNAP work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance rules, Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals due around Jan 2027) under a 75% state admin share and a 6% error cliff. Vendors test their own work. States rarely have independent, boundary-case test data with signed-off expected outcomes.
solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.

title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: High Mobility, agrirouter (cross-manufacturer agricultural data exchange), Jaltest / Cojali (Jaltest Diagnostics and Jaltest Telematics), OEM-owned platforms (KONE API portal; Otis ONE, Schindler Ahead and TK Elevator MAX are from my background knowledge and not verified this session). The verdict rests on direct page fetches and GitHub searches only, so treat 'gap' as moderate-to-low confidence. Re-run with the budget raised before committing money.

Within those limits, I found no product that files Data Act Article 4/5 requests on an equipment owner's behalf, tracks OEM responses, and normalises the returns across OEMs for independent service shops. Every adjacent player is either an OEM platform, cars-only (High Mobility), farmer-facing (agrirouter), on-site diagnostics (Jaltest), or OEM-side compliance code (GitHub kits). Genuinely unserved: (1) the owner-mandate plus request workflow, (2) an OEM-by-OEM response and refusal log, (3) a cross-OEM schema for lifts, heat pumps and forklifts, (4) the independent maintainer as the paying customer.

Structural weaknesses to fix in the idea:
- No fixed response deadline. As I recall Articles 4-5, data holders must respond 'without undue delay'. I could not fetch EUR-Lex to confirm (its WAF blocked me), but the idea's 'track statutory response deadlines' looks wrong.
- Article 5(1) lets 'a party acting on behalf of a user' request data. The independent shop can therefore file the request itself with a signed mandate. The broker's moat is then normalisation and OEM knowledge, not legal standing. Model letters and the Commission FAQ (v1.4, 22 Jan 2026) will commoditise the templates.
- Article 9 lets OEMs charge data recipients reasonable compensation, with a cost cap for SMEs, so OEMs may bill the shops you serve.
- Only 'readily available data' is covered. OEMs will argue that diagnostics are derived data, or invoke trade-secret and security refusals under Article 4(6)-(8). Safety-critical elevators are the likeliest place for a security argument.
- Article 4(1) design-by-default applies only to newly placed products, and old lifts often have no OEM connectivity.
- Tractors and other ag machinery may already have sector-specific repair-information access rules under type-approval law (Reg. 167/2013, from memory, unverified), which weakens ag as a beachhead.

title: Independent Collateral Verifier for Warehouse Lenders
one_liner: Sell the same listing-vs-ledger signal not to the floorplan lender but to the lender's lender: credit funds and banks that fund floorplan and subprime auto lenders and get a borrower-supplied VIN tape they have never been able to check, delivered as a signed monthly verification certificate that borrowers pay for through facility fees.
customer: Portfolio-monitoring and credit officers at credit funds, banks and specialty-finance desks that provide warehouse or revolving lines to independent floorplan companies and subprime or BHPH auto lenders. The chooser is the warehouse lender, and the payer is usually the borrower via a monitoring fee written into the facility, the way custodian and backup-servicer fees already are. The law firms that draft these credit agreements are a second influence channel.
problem: After Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025), the lender's lender is exposed to collateral that is self-reported by the party with the strongest incentive to overstate it. It receives a VIN-level borrowing-base tape weekly or monthly. It has no auditors and no view into dealers, and field exams are annual, sample-based and weeks stale. It holds the tape but has no line of outside data to check it against. Existing floorplan-side tools are bought by the borrower, so they cannot be independent by construction.
solution: Tape-in, verification-out. The warehouse lender (or borrower on its behalf) forwards the borrowing-base tape it already receives and we return a weekly exceptions report and a signed monthly Borrowing Base Verification Certificate. (1) VIN-level reconcile of every tape VIN against listing history and the borrower's reported paydowns and collections, flagging vanished-from-listing with no paydown. (2) A borrower-level Collateral Integrity Index covering percent of tape VINs vanished-unpaid by age bucket, listing coverage ratio, and trend, benchmarked against the warehouse lender's other borrowers. (3) Because noise averages out at portfolio level, precision required is far lower than for per-VIN dispatch, and low listing coverage is reported as its own finding, not hidden. (4) Escalation: a 'for-cause exam recommended' trigger with a shortlist of dealers for a partner field-exam firm. (5) Contract language kit: a standard 'independent verification agent' covenant and fee schedule for law firms to drop into new facilities and amendments.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put verification failure in front of every warehouse lender and investor. Private credit funds now hold large slices of specialty-auto warehouse exposure with small monitoring teams. Facilities are being re-papered and re-underwritten, so a verification covenant can go in now instead of waiting for a renewal cycle. Cheap licensed listing history and LLM tape parsing make a weekly external check a software job instead of an exam-firm engagement.
revenue_model: Monitoring fee of about $3,000 to $6,000 per facility per month ($36k to $72k per year), paid by the borrower through the facility's fee schedule or by the lender directly, plus a $15k to $25k onboarding backtest. Add-ons include a 10 to 15 percent referral fee from partner field-exam firms on for-cause exams, and licensing the anonymized Collateral Integrity Index to ABS investors and surveillance teams. If a niche of 100 to 150 specialty-auto warehouse lenders with 3 to 5 facilities each adopts it, the ceiling is roughly 300 to 600 facilities, or $15M to $30M per year before expanding to retail-auto tapes. These figures are assumptions to test.
non_obvious_insight: The funding-side buyer already owns the one input the product needs (the VIN tape) and has never had a single external data point to check it against. Verification fees are set by the chooser but paid by the borrower, who benefits from an independent stamp that supports better advance rates, so the payer wants it even when the chooser only tolerates it. Once written into facility documents, a fee line like custodian and backup servicer is sticky and renews automatically, which is a switching-cost moat that a per-dealer SaaS tool never gets.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 10, list 40 warehouse lenders and credit funds active in specialty auto from trade press and deal announcements, and line up conversations with two or three finance law partners who draft these facilities. Days 10 to 30, run 10 calls with portfolio monitoring heads and offer a free one-facility 'shadow verification' using a tape they already hold. They email it, and within five business days we return a one-page findings memo covering coverage ratio, vanished-unpaid VIN count and peer benchmark. Also sign a partner field-exam firm for for-cause follow-ups. Success is one lender agreeing to a paid quarter and one law firm agreeing to circulate the covenant language.

title: Independent Herd Audits for Loan Participation Buyers
one_liner: Charge the correspondent banks, credit unions and credit funds that buy pieces of cattle loans they cannot see, using sampling audits and a verified collateral tape sold through bankers' banks.
customer: The participation desk or chief credit officer at correspondent ag banks, credit unions and ag-focused credit funds that buy participations in cattle loans from community banks. Community banks hit legal lending limits and sell off big pieces of $2M+ herd loans. Channel partners are the bankers' banks that broker those participations. Later buyers are pool purchasers such as Farmer Mac-style secondary-market programs.
problem: A participant that owns 80-90% of a cattle loan has never seen the cattle. It relies on the lead bank's annual inspection, and the lead bank has already sold most of the risk, keeps servicing fees and has reason to want the loan to look clean. Participation agreements normally give buyers information and inspection rights, but the rights go unused because sending an inspector to a ranch two states away costs $1,500+ and buyers do not know how to audit a herd. The parent's fraud case (about $2.8M against 850 head, claimed and unverified) sits in the loan size that small banks typically participate out. That is a hypothesis to confirm.
solution: A 'Participation Audit' program sold to the buyer of risk, not the originator. Tier 1 desk audit ($300-500): a document reconciliation (sale-barn and brand records, tag and vet purchases) plus a lien search, compared against the lead bank's inspection report. Tier 2 ($1,200-2,000): adds a vet-attested chute-side scan or a credentialed field inspector, with geotagged photos and an EID or visual tag scan, timed to preg-check, weaning or a scheduled sale. Tier 3: surprise audit triggered by a lead-bank downgrade, a delinquency or a cattle-price drop. Buyers audit a random 15-25% of each pool every year, so every borrower knows the draw could land on them, which deters fraud. Buyers also get a verified collateral tape with loan-level fields (head, class, pregnancy rate, variance, lien position, date). That tape lets them price participations and lets funds bid for them. Bankers' banks embed the service in their participation platform for a 20-25% revenue share.
why_now: Herd rebuilding is debt-financed, so more cattle loans are being participated, and delinquencies are rising. A cattle-fraud headline (claimed in the parent, unverified) makes participants ask why they trust the lead bank's word. Examiner guidance generally expects participants to do their own credit analysis rather than lean on the lead, which is worth confirming with counsel. Non-bank capital has been moving into ag credit and needs diligence infrastructure. Remote document reconciliation makes a $400 Tier 1 audit profitable, where a field-only inspector could never be. Farm-loan stress typically creates an appetite for independent verification.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees: Tier 1 at about $400 and Tier 2 at about $1,500. Add $250/loan/year of monitoring, plus a 20-25% share to the bankers' bank. Data subscription for the verified collateral tape at $2-5K/month per buyer. Later, a 5-10 bps diligence fee on pool trades. Example: a correspondent buyer holding $150M across 150 cattle loans pays 150 x $400 + 38 Tier 2 audits x $1,500 + 150 x $250 = about $155K/yr. Ten such buyers is roughly $1.5M in recurring revenue. Field inspection labor is variable, using vet and tech partners paid per visit.
non_obvious_insight: In a participation, the party with the most money at risk has the least information and holds a contractual right that nobody uses because exercising it is operationally impossible. The buyer's question is not 'is the borrower honest' but 'is my lead bank's report honest'. Independence from the lead bank is therefore the product, and adverse selection disappears because the buyer picks the sample after buying, and randomness is the deterrent. Vets are optional at Tier 2, so vet reluctance no longer blocks the business.
first_30_days: Call 15 people: 5 bankers' banks and correspondent participation desks, 5 community-bank lead lenders that sell cattle participations, and 5 credit unions that buy them. Ask for the inspection clause in an actual participation agreement, whether anyone has ever inspected a participated cattle loan, who did it and what it cost. Find one buyer willing to pay $1,000 each for 5 participated cattle loans and invoke its inspection rights with the lead bank. Time the visits to fall preg-check or weaning days with two partner vets or field inspectors. Deliver five Tier 2 reports and a one-page comparison of what we found against the lead bank's file. Use that comparison to pitch a bankers' bank on adding the program to its participation platform.

title: Mixed-Lot Calf Referee With Brix Price Formulas
one_liner: An independent, photo-stamped Brix grade taken at the broker's loading dock that turns a blind mixed-dairy calf lot into a formula-priced lot, so the best dairies stop subsidizing the worst and disputes get settled by schedule, not argument.
customer: Wedge: independent calf brokers and sale-barn aggregators who assemble roughly 200-800 day 2-7 beef-on-dairy calves a week from 10-30 dairies and sell them to raisers who have no history with any of the source dairies. Start with 3-5 brokers in one dairy-dense region. Second payer: the raisers who buy those lots. Not the target: contracted dairy-to-ranch flows and integrated operators, where source reputation already does the job.
problem: Mixed-source lots are priced at a lemons discount. The buyer cannot tell which dairy's calves are good, so he pays for the average and hedges for the worst, and good dairies subsidize bad ones. Brokers eat 'adjustments' and lose a buyer after one bad lot. When calves die at the raiser, the dispute cannot be resolved: the dairy blames luck and the raiser blames the calves. A raiser can self-test for $1, but the seller will not accept the buyer's number, and the buyer will not accept the seller's, so measurement alone settles nothing. Packers already apply standardized deductions for unknown health history, so that discount is passed back upstream to brokers.
solution: 1) Two techs sample at unload or loading: every calf in lots sold as 'graded', a 20-calf random sample in standard lots. One phone frame captures ear tag, tube label and the refractometer display, timestamped and geotagged, so custody is the product. 2) Each calf is graded on the Lombard four-tier scale and the lot gets a score. 3) The lot quote carries a pre-agreed Settlement Schedule: a price add per Excellent/Good head, and an automatic per-head credit if Poor exceeds an agreed share of the lot (for example 30%). The buyer accepts or rejects at arrival by formula. This is a price term, not insurance or a warranty. 4) The broker uses the grades to split lots by dairy quality and sell the top tier at a spread. 5) The referee also holds the tag-level chain of custody for any 30-day death dispute (necropsy photo plus treatment log).
why_now: Crossbred calves at $1,000-1,500 make a 10-point mortality gap worth $100+ a head, so the number now matters to a broker's P&L. Feeders are being told not to assume a crossbred premium, so the market's question is shifting from 'what genetics' to 'which calves live'. The Lombard 2020 four-tier standard exists, digital refractometers cost about $150, and photo-stamped custody capture on a phone is now trivial to build. The same lot could not have been priced this way in 2019, when a calf was worth a fraction as much.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf, split between broker and buyer. In the first 90 days, success-based: the fee is due only on lots that clear at least $10 a head over the ungraded quote, so grading pays for itself before it bills. Add $75 per settlement or claim adjudication and a $250/month broker dashboard with a dairy league table. Honest sizing: 300 calves a week per broker is about $78K a year, so 15 brokers is about $1.2M. Test fees alone cap out in the low millions, so the wedge's real value is the custody dataset, which is the base for the guarantee and warranty layers in the other branches.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not the number, it is the pre-agreed price formula attached to it. Disclosure unravels (Grossman-Milgrom): once the two or three best dairies in a lot prove Excellent, any dairy that refuses grading gets priced as Poor, so you only have to win the best sellers rather than the whole market. And no buyer needs to state a premium: the money is the lemons discount already being taken out of good calves in mixed lots, which sidesteps the 'no proven crossbred premium' headwind.
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit one broker or sale barn moving 300+ calves a week, and pick their 3 best dairies (the ones who want to prove it). Buy two refractometers, tubes and centrifuge or clot rack, and set up a photo-stamp capture form on a no-code tool. Weeks 2-4: grade every calf free at loading (about 1,200 calves), send lot sheets and a proposed Settlement Schedule to 2-3 buyers, and ask them to report 30-day illness and death by ear tag. Day 45 go/no-go gates: (a) at least one buyer signs a schedule with a spread of $25 or more a head between Good-or-better and Poor; (b) Poor calves show at least 1.5x the 30-day loss of Excellent/Good. If either fails, stop. Before spending on anything else, verify the 10-25% raiser-loss figure from the parent, since it is unsourced.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

Calftech-style integrated ranches keep data in-house because they own both sides; this only sells into unintegrated trade (mixed lots), and an integrated operator buying outside calves becomes a customer. Bilateral-history substitution is avoided by targeting only lots where no history exists. Warranty moral hazard is avoided because nothing here insures the raiser's management.

title: Outside-In Product Security Ratings for Insurers and Buyers
one_liner: Invert the desk: instead of helping one maker meet the 24-hour clock, independently measure from the outside whether thousands of connected-product makers can, and how exposed their shipped firmware is, and sell the scores and accumulation data to insurers, fleet buyers and lenders.
customer: First buyers: cyber and product-liability insurers and MGAs writing hardware and IoT makers, who need product-level exposure and accumulation data. Second: B2B fleet and infrastructure buyers (EV-charging operators, micromobility fleets, smart-building integrators, telcos buying CPE) that run supplier due diligence. Third: lenders and PE firms doing diligence on hardware brands. Manufacturers do not buy scores. They pay only for evidence review and remediation (a funnel to the desk).
problem: Every maker will soon say 'we comply' with the CRA, but the declarations are self-assessed and unverified until a market surveillance authority acts, which is slow and under-resourced. Insurers have no product-level model of accumulation, even though one exploited component hits every device on that stack. That is a catastrophe-modelling problem with no model. Procurement teams rely on questionnaires. The 24-hour clock is uniquely measurable: it is a dated, binary behaviour, unlike vague 'security posture', but nobody measures it from outside.
solution: A rating built outside-in from three layers. (a) Clock-readiness signals: security.txt, a published CVD policy, a working vulnerability contact, advisory history, stated support period, update cadence, and time-to-acknowledge on a clearly labelled contact-verification probe. (b) Firmware exposure: public firmware and OTA images, plus purchased units for top SKUs, unpacked and matched against exploited-vulnerability feeds to give a component list, exposure count and stack cluster. (c) Portfolio accumulation: for an insurer's book of insureds or a fleet buyer's supplier list, how many share a stack with a newly exploited component (the correlation number). Makers get a right of reply and can submit evidence, but cannot pay to change a score. Method: month 0-3 process-signal ratings for about 500 brands across e-mobility, smart home, routers, chargers, cameras and wearables; month 3-6 firmware exposure on the top 200 SKUs and the first accumulation reports. A separate analyst team runs the desk as the remediation upsell, behind a conflict-of-interest firewall.
why_now: The reporting duty went live on 11 Sep 2026, so 'time to report' just became a legal, checkable behaviour. Insurers are pricing CRA-driven product liability for the first time. Outside-in ratings are a proven category for company networks, and firmware unpacking is now cheap through open-source tooling and LLM-assisted triage. No dominant product-level rating exists.
revenue_model: Data licences of EUR 25-80k/yr per insurer or MGA; EUR 6-15k/yr per fleet operator or integrator per category; EUR 3-8k per diligence report for lenders and PE; EUR 2-5k per maker for evidence review; desk upsell as a funnel. Long term the rating is written into insurance pricing and procurement clauses ('supplier must hold a score of B or better'), giving standard-setter economics with a data moat.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers care about accumulation more than any single score, and the desk's pooled stack graph is exactly an accumulation model, so the same data serves the desk and the rating. Real filings and drills, with consent and anonymised, give a calibration set showing which outside-in signals predict actual time-to-report, and that validation is what makes a rating credible. Every desk client both funds and calibrates the rating. Flaw of the inversion: legal risk (defamation, unauthorised access), which is why probes are labelled, analysis uses lawfully obtained units and public images, scores are aggregated and methodology is public.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a crawler over 500 brands in 6 categories to score security.txt, CVD page, contact deliverability, advisory history and support-period statements. Week 2: send a benign, clearly labelled contact-verification probe and record response times. Week 3: publish a free report, 'State of vulnerability-reporting readiness among 500 connected-product brands' (for example, what share have no working vulnerability contact weeks after the duty began), to earn press and insurer attention. Weeks 3-4: hold 20 discovery calls with cyber/product-liability underwriters, MGAs and fleet operators, and offer paid pilots of EUR 8-15k to score their insureds or suppliers. Aim for one signed pilot by day 45 and confirm that no insurer-grade product rating already exists before scaling.
