Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors (Finite State, Cybellum, ONEKEY, Cybeats, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, CRACI) all work inside-out for the manufacturer's own firmware or workflow and are paid by the maker. This business is outside-in and paid by the party that bears the risk, so none of them competes for that buyer, and several become data suppliers. From general knowledge, not verified in this session: company-level ratings such as BitSight and SecurityScorecard score networks, not shipped products; certification schemes (ioXt, ETSI EN 303 645-based tests, UL programmes) are pass/fail, point-in-time and manufacturer-paid; consumer-testing NGOs publish periodic tests. Large MSSPs and certification bodies are conflicted because manufacturers pay them. The moat is the calibrated stack graph, the methodology and eventual adoption in insurance and procurement contracts.

title: Dual-Mode Genset Permits for Queued Campuses
one_liner: Design the air permit for new data center campuses before the generators are bought, so the backup fleet is legally curtailment-ready from day one and the fee is tied to energization date.
customer: Energy and development leads at spec developers, powered-shell builders and neocloud/colo operators with 50-400 MW campuses in PJM (AEP Ohio, Dominion, ComEd, PPL). The wedge is campuses that have filed, or are about to file, their air-permit application and have not yet placed genset purchase orders. Hyperscalers with in-house permitting teams are excluded at first. Air consultants are a secondary channel.
problem: The parent's real cost is retrofitting existing Tier 2 emergency fleets. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), emergency engines are capped at 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of that can earn income or serve a financial arrangement. Reclassifying an installed fleet means stricter engine standards, re-permitting and public comment. Yet the largest cohort of new engines is being permitted right now as emergency-only, because that is the cheapest and fastest path. That choice locks out capacity and curtailment use for 15 or more years. PJM's curtail-or-bring-capacity direction means those same campuses will need on-site backup to energize earlier. Nobody is designing the permit for that second use at the moment the choice is cheap.
solution: A fixed-price 'Dual-Mode Permit Package' sold before genset purchase orders and inside the air-permit comment window. (1) A one-time state legal feasibility memo from a retained air attorney (VA, OH, IL, PA), which gates every engagement. (2) An engine spec that is Tier 4 Final or SCR-ready, with catalyst and urea footprint reserved, ECM hour-metering and paralleling ready. This turns retrofit financing into a spec change costing a fraction of a retrofit. (3) Permit application language and modeling: an emergency mode plus a capped grid-emergency/curtailment mode of roughly 100-200 hours, synthetic-minor NOx limits, 1-hour NO2 dispersion modeling, and a community disclosure plan. (4) A curtailment-readiness dossier the utility and PJM can cite when offering earlier or flexible energization. Engines are certified as non-emergency-capable from the start, so the campus never has to fight the emergency-to-non-emergency reclassification.
why_now: Turbines are sold out until roughly 2029-30, so the practical path to earlier energization is on-site capacity that can be built now. PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short, and the connect-and-manage and bring-your-own-capacity framework is being filed at FERC. Large OEM gensets with SCR options are catalog items, and campuses energizing in 2028-30 must order engines and file permits in the next 6-12 months. This would not have worked in 2019, when there was no curtailment penalty for missing on-site capacity.
revenue_model: $60-150k fixed fee per campus (feasibility memo, spec, permit drafting, modeling). A success fee applies when the permit issues with the dual-mode condition (about $50k), and a further one applies only when the utility or PJM offers earlier or flexible energization that cites the dossier, at roughly $1-2k per MW per month of acceleration. A 200 MW campus energized six months early is worth about $1-2M to us. A colo campus that size earns on the order of $30M a month at full lease-up, so the buyer's return is 50x or more. An optional 10% share of capacity revenue for five years is secondary. Illustrative unit economics: 10 campuses in year one is roughly $1.5-3M, with two lawyers, two engineers and one permit modeler.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest time to unlock diesel is before it exists. The permit design is a one-time, 15-year decision, and taking it at application costs a fraction of a retrofit. It turns the parent's hardest problem (retrofit financing plus reclassification risk) into a purchase-spec problem that the buyer is already paying for. It also changes what is being sold, from capacity revenue that the buyer discounts to time. Energization date is the metric a developer's CFO already tracks, and every month of delay costs more than any capacity payment. Public permit dockets show exactly which campuses are in the window, so lead generation is a scrape rather than cold outreach.
first_30_days: Week 1: commission the air-attorney feasibility memo ($8-10k), covering which engine and classification path works in VA, OH, IL and PA. If no path closes at Tier 4 or SCR cost, stop. Weeks 1-2: scrape VA DEQ, Ohio EPA, IEPA and PA DEP public notices for data center genset permit applications filed in the last 12 months (target 40) and identify the developer and the consultant of record for each. Weeks 2-4: cold-contact the development leads and offer a $12k 'dual-mode gap review' of the pending application inside the public comment window. In parallel, offer the applicants' air consultants a white-label subcontract for the dual-mode module. Aim for two paid gap reviews and one campus package LOI. The demand test is whether a developer will pay before PO to keep the option open.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Trinity-type consultancies sell reactive, hourly permit work, are not tied to capacity or energization outcomes, and do not spec engines. We offer them the dual-mode module as a white-label add-on rather than compete. Voltus and CPower can only enroll resources that are already dual-mode, so we are their upstream and never touch enrollment or the DR revenue relationship. ERock sells gas hardware and a bridge-to-grid story. We are engine-agnostic and ride on gensets the campus must buy anyway, so there is no incremental hardware capex to finance. We also avoid the parent's unproven retrofit-of-Tier-2 step and its legal trap by working only on greenfield permits, and we gate on the attorney memo.

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.

Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.

title: Rural Sales Commons: Pay Retiring Appraisers for Comps
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of retirees paying to leave, pay them for their verified sales books and build the private sales-price registry that non-disclosure states lack, sold first to practicing rural appraisers and later to AVM, lender and assessor buyers.
customer: Supply (paid): retiring and retired certified residential appraisers in roughly a dozen non-disclosure states (for example TX, UT, ID, MT, WY, NM, KS, LA, MS, ND), starting with Texas. Demand: practicing rural appraisers first (subscription), then AVM and hybrid-valuation vendors, rural lenders' collateral-risk teams, county assessors for ratio studies, and eventually programs expanding alternative valuations.
problem: In non-disclosure states, sale prices are not in public deed records. For non-MLS rural sales (FSBO, family transfers, auctions, seller-financed land-with-house), the only record of price is often an appraiser's own phone-confirmation notes and comp files. When the appraiser retires, that sales book is thrown out or dies on a hard drive. Practicing appraisers then struggle to find defensible comps, AVMs and desktop valuations are weakest exactly there (hypothesis to test), and human appraisers stay indispensable and scarce.
solution: Wedge product: a 'Rural Comp Finder' subscription for practicing appraisers in one region, built from a paid capture program. (1) Sales Book Capture: a 2-day white-glove engagement in which we ingest the retiree's comp libraries (a la mode or ClickFORMS exports, spreadsheets, paper binders) with LLM parsing. We keep only transaction facts (date, price, terms, property characteristics, verification source and method), plus the retiree's own adjustment grids and market-area notes. Client and borrower identities never enter the system, and MLS-derived fields are tagged and excluded. The retiree signs a license and certifies what is theirs. (2) Product: county-level search showing each verified sale with provenance (who confirmed, how, when) and a confidence grade, plus a paired-sales adjustment library. (3) Contributor loop: active appraisers who add confirmed sales get a discount, so the commons refreshes after the retirees are gone. (4) Later products: API and data licenses to AVM and hybrid vendors, lenders and county assessors, positioned as ground truth for validating AVMs and alternative valuations.
why_now: About 6-7k appraisers a year are expected to leave (31% of a roughly 65k workforce within 3 years per WorkingRE), and each exit destroys a sales book permanently. UAD 3.6 (mandatory Nov 2, 2026) pushes the industry toward structured data. EO 14393 expands alternative valuations, which need ground truth in thin markets. LLM extraction of messy comp files (old exports, PDFs, handwritten binders) became cheap enough in 2025-26 to make capture affordable.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $39-59 per month per region for active appraisers (contributors pay less). Data licenses of about $25-120k per state per year to AVM and hybrid vendors and lenders, and $15-40k per year to assessors (all unvalidated). Retirees are paid $1,500-3,000 upfront plus a 20-25% royalty pool shared by verified contribution, and that payout is our main cost of goods. Rough plan (assumptions): 20 retirees x about $2,000 is $40k to acquire perhaps 50-100k verified records. 300 subscribers by month 12 is roughly $210k ARR before any data licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks retirees to pay, but a retiree is a supplier with a ticking clock. Each exit permanently deletes an asset that no later entrant can recreate, and scraping cannot reach it because the value is provenance: who confirmed this price, how and when. First to sign the last generation of phone-confirming appraisers cornered a resource competitors cannot buy once it is gone. Practicing appraisers contributing new confirmed sales gives the commons a network effect that outlasts the retirees. The moat is the counsel-designed data model (provenance tagging, MLS exclusion, client stripping), which turns legal risk into a barrier to fast followers. Because retirees are paid, the parent's unproven willingness-to-pay problem disappears and no earn-out or client transfer is needed.
first_30_days: Gating step: a counsel memo on MLS license terms, the USPAP Confidentiality Rule, GLBA and state board views, and stop or redesign if the extractable data set is too thin. Interview 15 retirees and 15 active appraisers in Texas and ask to see their comp books. Buy 5 sales books at $1,500 as paid pilots, parse them with an LLM pipeline, and tag provenance and MLS-derived rows. Run a blind coverage test on one rural county: how many verified non-MLS sales in the last 5 years the commons holds versus what an active appraiser or an AVM can find. Show the test to 3 AVM or hybrid-valuation vendors and 3 rural lenders and ask for letters of intent. Pre-sell a $39 per month beta to 30 active appraisers. Because the web-search budget ran out, also verify in week 1 whether Cotality, ATTOM or any appraiser comp-sharing group already sells verified non-MLS sales in non-disclosure states.

USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.

Incumbent data vendors (Cotality, ATTOM, MLS aggregators) depend on MLS feeds and recorder data and would have to buy retiree confirmations one appraiser at a time, which does not fit their scale (unverified, to check in week 1). The design avoids fee-splitting law because no appraisal fee or client revenue is shared, avoids supervisor-licensing issues, and avoids weak client transferability because no clients move.

title: Pooled Calendar Reporters for Limited-Scope Family Lawyers
one_liner: One physically present reporter sits an entire family-court calendar and sells the record by the matter, about $110 per 15-minute hearing, so each lawyer pays roughly 75% less than a half-day pro tem while the reporter earns more than a normal pro tem day.
customer: Wedge: limited-scope (unbundled) and solo family-law attorneys who appear on DVRO, custody and support calendars in ONE high-volume California courthouse, plus the non-indigent 'missing middle' litigants they represent, who fail the fee-waiver test but cannot spend $450 on a record. Not indigent litigants (the FVAP ruling moves them to a court-paid record) and not the court.
problem: About 7 in 10 civil, family and probate hearings in California have no verbatim record, and appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail without one. Courts tell litigants to 'arrange your own' reporter, but a private pro tem costs $450-500 for a half day, and no one pays that for a 12-minute item. The parent's fix (remote reporters dialing in) is barred by Gov. Code 69959 and by the 69959.5 pilot limits, so it cannot launch as written. The parent also has no proof that anyone will pay $95, and the ruling shrinks the legal-aid segment.
solution: Drop remote reporting and prediction. A reporter is physically in the department for the whole morning or afternoon calendar, which is the lawful 'bring your own reporter' route. Attorneys book a matter slot the day before at $110 for up to 15 minutes, plus a per-page certified transcript (about $8/page) only if they order one. Booking is all-or-nothing, like a crowdfund: the reporter goes only if at least 6-8 matters are booked by 5pm the day before, otherwise everyone is refunded. That kills the dead-time problem without any duration model. Each party gets only its own matter's transcript, and other matters on the reporter's notes are never released. Cross-department hopping and duration prediction come later, once the manual logs give real data. Unit economics (assumptions to test): 2 sessions/day x 8 matters x $110 = $1,760 gross. The reporter keeps about 60% ($1,056) versus $900-1,000 for two half-day pro tem bookings, and the company keeps about $700 per reporter-day before ops.
why_now: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) put the 70% no-record gap in every family lawyer's inbox. It also makes courts serve only indigent litigants, which leaves a large paying middle. Courts are already telling family litigants in writing to arrange their own reporter. The reporter shortage (about 5,500 short by 2030) means freelancers can choose better-paying days, so a higher-yield day is a real recruiting pitch.
revenue_model: $110 per matter slot for up to 15 minutes, $8/page for certified transcripts, and prepaid 5-packs ($500) for cash up front. The reporter keeps about 60% of slot fees, the platform keeps about 40% (about 35% gross margin after the payment and ops costs of a services business). Year-2 add-ons: a subscription for attorneys who book 8+ hearings a month, and referral-funded 'record scholarships' from DV appellate nonprofits.
non_obvious_insight: Once the first attorney in a department triggers the reporter's presence, every other matter that day costs roughly nothing extra, so the price can fall 75% while the reporter's day pay rises. Limited-scope attorneys are the right buyer because they bill flat per hearing and can pass the record fee through as an itemized line, while a full-service litigator does not think of the record as a per-hearing line item. The tipping-point booking rule replaces the prediction model the parent needed.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney and the clerks of the 2 target departments (private pro tem in the room, multiple parties sharing one reporter, closed-hearing rules, and any court-reporting-firm registration). Weeks 1-2: pick the single biggest family courthouse in one county, recruit 3 physically local pro tem reporters, and pre-sell 5-packs to 15 limited-scope attorneys from the family-law bar and unbundled-services listservs. Weeks 3-4: run the first 10 calendars with a Google Sheet, Stripe links and a group text, using the booking threshold, and log booked-matter density and actual call order per department. Offer FVAP and one DV appellate nonprofit free slots for cases they flag as appeal-bound.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep, StenoScout and the agencies (Veritext, Esquire and others) sell a whole appearance to one buyer, mostly depositions, so every buyer pays the full minimum, and their half-day minimum is structural. We sell the matter, split one appearance across many paying parties, and stay lawful without remote reporting. The AB 3013 pilot covers only court-employed reporters in a court facility, capped at 10-20% of reporters in 13 counties. We serve paying litigants in any county and do not compete for the court-employed slots. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings, which fits the court's indigent fallback but not an attorney who wants a stenographic record, live and immediate. The moat, if the wedge works, is proprietary calendar density and call-order data per department, and reporter loyalty from the higher day yield, which points to a cornered-resource advantage in one courthouse before any scale.

title: Lead Line Photos Taken During Meter Swaps
one_liner: Add a 90-second, three-photo service-entry protocol with on-device AI to the water-meter change-out crews a utility already sends into basements, and sell it to the utility as a $10-14 per line change order.
customer: Mid-size water utilities (30k-150k connections) in the Northeast and Great Lakes that have inside-set meters, an active or planned meter or AMI replacement program, and more than 30% 'unknown' service lines in their inventory. Two budget owners: the AMI/meter program manager (capital project change order) and the lead program manager (compliance budget). The meter-installation contractor is the channel and co-beneficiary. Wedge account: a utility whose meter contractor has not yet mobilized, so the protocol goes into the statement of work.
problem: Unknown lines stay unknown because access is the hard part. Mailer self-ID reaches 10-25% of owners, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. The parent idea's paid-photo network has three weak points. First, opportunistic supply (home sales, water-heater swaps) is thin per utility. Second, the state may treat photos from third parties as self-ID-grade evidence, because the rule appears to require identification by 'water system personnel' (verify by state). Third, inspectors may not accept the liability of calling a pipe lead. Meanwhile utilities are paying crews to enter the very same basements and stand within about 3 feet of the service entry for every inside meter swap. Those crews record a meter serial and nothing about the pipe.
solution: An app or SDK for the meter crew. Photo 1 shows the pipe where it enters the wall, upstream of the meter valve. Photo 2 is a scratch and magnet close-up, using a $0.50 test card in the installer's kit. Photo 3 shows the meter serial and pipe together, which ties the evidence to the account. On-device checks reject blurry or ambiguous shots while the tech is still standing there ('retake, pipe not visible'). A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, plastic or unresolved. Low-confidence cases go to human QA and, for unresolved or mixed-material lines, to a probe or pothole queue. The tech never labels a pipe, which removes the liability concern. Output is a reconciled inventory feed in the state portal format, pushed into the utility's Esri layer, plus a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP. Techs get a small per-verified-set bonus so they don't skip the step.
why_now: Meter fleets from the 2000s-2010s AMR wave are hitting battery and end-of-life, and cellular sunsets have pushed utilities into funded AMI change-outs (verify local schedules). These are the few funded programs that put a utility contractor inside every home in a specific neighborhood. State inventory updates and the 10-year replacement clock (federal details are still being litigated and revisited, and several states have their own statutes) mean unknowns carry real cost and a deadline. On-device vision models now catch bad photos at capture time, so the crew does not have to be an expert. SRF and infrastructure-law money rewards utilities that shrink unknowns before applying for replacement funds.
revenue_model: Per-line fee of $10-14 billed as a change order to the meter deployment contract, or as a per-utility deployment license of $60-150k. Change orders in that size range often clear without a council vote. Rough unit economics per line: installer bonus $2-3, kit $0.50, AI and QA $2-3, hosting and support about $1, leaving about $5-6 gross margin (roughly 45%). A 40k-inside-meter deployment is about $480k of revenue. Add-ons: inventory reconciliation SaaS, and later a resell of the same feed to meter contractors as a bundled 'verification-ready' option in their bids.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a photographer, it is legal access. Every water tariff already makes meter access a condition of service, and utilities enforce it with repeat visits and shutoff notices, so meter crews reach exactly the absentee-landlord and LLC homes that no self-ID portal can reach, at a marginal trip cost of zero. The crew is also water system personnel or contractor, so the evidence sits in the strongest evidentiary class the state rule seems to allow. And the pipe at an inside-set meter is usually the same pipe the lead rule cares about, a few feet from where the crew is already working. A separate paid-photo marketplace has to build access, supply and trust. This borrows all three from the utility's own procurement.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every utility in two states that has inside meters, an announced meter or AMI program, and a public inventory over 30% unknown. Call the AMI program manager and the lead program manager at 15 of them. Also call three meter-installation contractors and ask whether they'd add a photo step for a per-set bonus. Days 10-20: get one state drinking-water program to say in writing whether a visual verification by utility-contracted personnel can reclassify an unknown. Prototype the capture app with real-time retake prompts and a scratch and magnet card. Days 20-30: run a 300-home pilot inside one utility's existing swap route, priced at cost as a change order. Validate the classifier against 100 lines the utility already knows (historical records, prior replacements) and against 20-30 potholes. Publish the accuracy and per-line cost, and propose a full-route contract at $12.
lineage: mutation of I0463 ('Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. This produces deterministic evidence for 100% of the homes the crew visits and can be sold to them as calibration data. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and the Chesterfield and Massachusetts DEP forms all depend on owners responding, and they reach 10-25%. Tariff-backed meter access is a lever they do not have. RCAP door-to-door inspections, Electro Scan probes and Echologics/Mueller acoustic tools all need a dedicated visit or crew per line. This rides a trip that is already paid for. Stantec and other engineering firms bill field crews hourly, so a $12 add-on cannibalizes their revenue and they are more likely to resell it than build it. Trinnex or Esri adding a contractor role would not reach into the meter-deployment workflow, which the installers and utilities own. The parent's inspector network is dropped as the primary channel, which removes the cold-start, the liability objection and the third-party evidence problem.

title: Scribe-Safe Billing: White-Label Audit for Billing Companies
one_liner: Outsourced billing companies buy a per-provider, coder-signed drift monitor and quarterly attestation letter, then resell it to their small-practice clients as 'scribe-safe billing'.
customer: Mid-size outsourced billing and RCM companies (roughly 40-500 providers under management, spread across 5-50 small groups, for example HBMA members) that bill for practices using a mix of scribes. Later channels: practice-management and EHR marketplaces, and IPAs.
problem: The bulk of scribe adoption in small practices is cheap or low-cost tooling with no compliance officer behind it. The billing company sees every claim across many clients and scribe vendors, is paid a percentage of collections (so scribe uplift raises its own fee), and can be exposed as a party that caused false claims. Its contract says the client owns documentation, but that does not stop a payer or DOJ from asking the biller what it did. Enterprise audit platforms are priced and sold for organizations with in-house compliance staff, so this segment gets nothing. Small groups also lack the resources to appeal payer downcodes.
solution: 'Scribe-Safe' program the biller white-labels. (1) Claims-only monitor across the biller's whole book, with no EHR access: per-provider E/M and modifier drift versus specialty peers, plus the payer downcode rate from 835 remits (CARC 150, 'payer deems the information does not support this level of service') as a leading signal. (2) Quarterly coder-signed review of about 8 encounters per flagged provider, focused on MDM and total-time statements. (3) A signed quarterly attestation letter per practice that the biller can show a client, payer or auditor. (4) A contract addendum plus a refund workflow so findings reach the practice's designated contact and can be acted on within the 60-day overpayment rule, so the biller never sits on an identified problem. (5) Cross-book benchmark by scribe vendor and specialty returned to the biller as a sales asset.
why_now: Small groups adopted low-cost scribes in 2025-26, payers' automated downcoding programs are now hitting the small groups least able to appeal, outsourced billing keeps growing, and billing companies compete on differentiation as AI coding commoditizes their core work. Law-firm commentary warns that 'the AI suggested it' is not a defense. Billing companies now need something independent to point to.
revenue_model: Wholesale $12-20 per provider per month; the biller resells at $25-40 or bundles it for retention. $25 per encounter for extra coder reviews. A 300-provider biller is about $45-70k a year, so 25 billers is roughly $1.1-1.75M ARR. Coder time is about $7 per provider per month at 8 reviews per quarter of about 6 minutes each with an AI pre-read, giving 55-65% gross margin. Land through a 60-day paid pilot at $4-6k per biller.
non_obvious_insight: The payer's own downcode rate is a free, externally labeled audit signal. A jump in CARC 150 adjustments for one provider after go-live means the payer's model has already flagged the notes, before any human looks. The billing company is also the only actor with a cross-client, cross-scribe view, and it buys cover more than detection: an independent signature is the product, which is why more AI coding automation is not a substitute.
first_30_days: Contact HBMA chapter leaders and 40 billing-company owners on LinkedIn. Offer a 60-day paid pilot ($4-6k) that starts with a scan of the biller's aggregated 12-month 837/835 book, structured under the biller's counsel and with the findings routed to practices, not left with the biller. Recruit 2 CPC/CPMA contractors and a healthcare lawyer to draft the addendum and refund workflow. Deliver a provider watchlist and 30 coder-signed reviews to each pilot. Goal: 3 signed pilots and 1 conversion to a per-provider contract.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: new-customer-or-model
